title: Top 5 Behavioural Interview Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
author: PlacementDo Team
excerpt: Behavioural questions trip up even experienced candidates. Here are the five most common mistakes — and the simple fixes that will make your answers stand out.
content:
# 5 Behavioural Interview Mistakes to Stop Making Today

Behavioural interviews are designed to predict how you will perform in a role based on how you have handled situations in the past. Yet most candidates walk in underprepared.

## Mistake 1 — Telling instead of showing

Saying "I am a great team player" means nothing without evidence. Use the STAR framework (Situation, Task, Action, Result) to anchor every answer in a specific, real story.

## Mistake 2 — Skipping the result

Interviewers want to know the outcome. Always finish your answer with a measurable result: "We shipped two weeks early" or "Customer satisfaction scores rose by 18%."

## Mistake 3 — Only preparing positive stories

Questions like "Tell me about a time you failed" are almost guaranteed. Have two or three honest failure stories ready, each ending with what you learned and changed.

## Mistake 4 — Rambling

The ideal STAR answer runs 90–120 seconds. Practise out loud so you know when to stop. PlacementDo reports include a response-length metric to help you calibrate.

## Mistake 5 — Ignoring the job description

Every company highlights the behaviours they value most in their job postings. Map your stories to those competencies before the interview.

## Practice makes permanent

The best way to fix these mistakes is deliberate repetition with feedback. Run a PlacementDo session, review the AI feedback, then re-record the same answer. Most users see measurable improvement within five practice sessions.

content:
# Complete Campus Placement Preparation Guide for 2026

Campus placements are the first big career milestone for most engineering and MBA graduates. Companies visit college campuses between August and February, and the competition is fierce. This guide walks you through every stage — from the aptitude pre-filter to the final HR round — so you arrive prepared.

## Understanding the placement process

Most companies follow a four-stage funnel:

- Online aptitude and reasoning test
- Technical written or coding round
- Technical interview (one or two panels)
- HR interview

The exact format varies by company and role, but preparing for each stage systematically keeps you in contention regardless of which firm visits first.

## Stage 1 — Aptitude and reasoning

The online test screens out a large percentage of candidates, so do not underestimate it. Focus on:

- Quantitative aptitude: percentages, ratios, time-speed-distance, work-time problems
- Logical reasoning: puzzles, syllogisms, blood relations, seating arrangements
- Verbal ability: reading comprehension, sentence correction, vocabulary

Practise 30 to 40 questions daily for three weeks before the season starts. Timed mock tests matter more than untimed practice because the actual test is always time-pressured.

## Stage 2 — Technical written or coding round

For software roles, expect one to three coding problems ranging from easy to medium difficulty. Core topics include:

- Arrays, strings, and hashmaps
- Linked lists, stacks, and queues
- Recursion and dynamic programming basics
- SQL queries and database design fundamentals

For non-software roles, this stage is typically a written test on core engineering subjects or a case study.

## Stage 3 — Technical interview

Interviewers test conceptual depth, problem-solving process, and communication. Common topics:

- Data structures and algorithm complexity
- Object-oriented design principles
- Operating systems and computer networks fundamentals
- Projects from your resume — be ready to explain every line

Think out loud when solving problems. Interviewers give partial credit for a clear thought process even when the final answer is incomplete.

## Stage 4 — HR interview

The HR round is not a formality. Recruiters are assessing culture fit, communication skills, and attitude. Prepare answers for:

- Tell me about yourself
- Why do you want to work here?
- Where do you see yourself in five years?
- Describe a challenge you overcame

Practise these aloud — not in your head. PlacementDo mock HR sessions let you rehearse with an AI interviewer and get instant feedback on clarity and confidence.

## Building a placement timeline

- Three months before: strengthen aptitude and DSA fundamentals
- Two months before: build two solid project descriptions from your resume
- One month before: run daily mock interviews, refine HR answers
- One week before: company-specific research and light revision

## Final tips

Track every company that visits, note their test pattern, and prioritise accordingly. Most importantly, stay consistent — companies often give offers within 24 hours of the final round, so momentum matters more than cramming at the last minute.

title: How to Write a Winning Resume for Freshers: Tips and Template
author: PlacementDo Team
excerpt: A recruiter spends an average of seven seconds on a fresher resume. Here is how to make every second count — from layout and keywords to project descriptions that get callbacks.
content:
# How to Write a Winning Resume for Freshers

A recruiter spends an average of seven seconds scanning a resume before deciding whether to continue reading. For freshers without years of work experience, that first impression is everything. This guide shows you exactly what to include, what to cut, and how to structure your one-page resume for maximum impact.

## The golden rule: one page

Freshers should keep their resume to one page. Hiring managers at large companies receive hundreds of applications; a concise, well-organized single page signals clarity of thought and respect for the reader's time.

## Essential sections and their order

### 1. Contact information

Place your name prominently at the top. Include your phone number, a professional email address (first.last@gmail.com, not gamer123@), and links to your LinkedIn profile and GitHub if relevant. Avoid a full home address — city and state are sufficient.

### 2. Summary or objective (optional but powerful)

Three lines that answer: who you are, what you can do, and what you are looking for. Tailor this to each role. Example: "Final-year Computer Science student with strong DSA fundamentals and two internship projects in full-stack development. Seeking a software engineering role where I can contribute to scalable products from day one."

### 3. Education

List your degree, institution, graduation year, and GPA or percentage if above 7.5 CGPA or 75%. Add relevant coursework if space allows.

### 4. Skills

Group skills logically: Programming Languages, Frameworks, Tools and Platforms, and Soft Skills. List only skills you can discuss confidently in an interview — do not pad this section.

### 5. Projects

This is the most important section for freshers. For each project:

- State what the project does in one sentence
- Describe your specific contribution (not just the team's)
- Quantify the result where possible: "Reduced API response time by 40%" beats "Improved performance"
- Link to a live demo or GitHub repository

Three strong projects beat six vague ones.

### 6. Internships and work experience

If you have internships, list them above projects. Use action verbs: built, designed, automated, reduced, improved. Focus on outcomes, not responsibilities.

### 7. Certifications and achievements

Include only relevant certifications (AWS, Google, Coursera courses in your domain) and notable achievements (hackathon wins, competitive programming rankings, academic medals).

## Formatting rules that matter

- Use a clean, ATS-friendly font: Calibri, Arial, or Georgia at 10–11pt
- Consistent margins: 0.5 to 0.75 inches
- Use bullet points, not paragraphs
- No photos, graphics, or tables — they confuse ATS software
- Export as PDF unless the job posting specifies Word

## Common mistakes freshers make

- Listing "MS Office" as a skill in 2026
- Using a generic objective statement
- Cramming five projects with no detail instead of two projects with clear impact
- Spelling the company name wrong in a tailored summary

## Tailoring your resume for each application

Before submitting, match your skills and project descriptions to the keywords in the job description. ATS filters look for exact or near-exact matches. Spending five minutes tailoring each application significantly improves your callback rate.

Once your resume is ready, practise talking about every line with PlacementDo — interviewers will probe the exact projects and skills you listed.

title: Top 30 HR Interview Questions and How to Answer Them
author: PlacementDo Team
excerpt: The HR interview is often the final gate before an offer. Master these 30 most-asked questions — with framework answers — and you will walk in with real confidence.
content:
# Top 30 HR Interview Questions and How to Answer Them

The HR interview is frequently the last round before an offer is made, yet candidates often prepare for it least. This is a mistake — HR interviewers are skilled at detecting rehearsed, hollow answers. The goal is to sound authentic while still being concise and structured.

## About yourself and background

### 1. Tell me about yourself

Give a 90-second career story: your educational background, a key project or experience, your core strength, and what you are looking for in your next role. Do not recite your resume.

### 2. Walk me through your resume

Highlight the two or three experiences most relevant to this role and explain the logical progression. Show intentionality, not just chronology.

### 3. What are your greatest strengths?

Pick two genuine strengths and back each with a specific example. Avoid generic answers like "hard worker" or "team player" without evidence.

### 4. What is your biggest weakness?

Choose a real weakness that is not critical to the role, describe the concrete step you are taking to address it, and mention early signs of improvement.

### 5. Why should we hire you?

Link your specific skills and experiences directly to the job requirements. End with enthusiasm for the role and company.

## Motivation and culture fit

### 6. Why do you want to work here?

Research the company's mission, products, culture, and recent news. Reference something specific that genuinely interests you — not just "it is a great company."

### 7. Where do you see yourself in five years?

Show ambition balanced with realism. Align your growth goal with the career path the company offers.

### 8. What motivates you at work?

Be honest. Common genuine motivators: solving complex problems, continuous learning, making a measurable impact, or working in a collaborative team.

### 9. How do you handle pressure and tight deadlines?

Describe a real high-pressure situation, your approach (prioritisation, communication, focused execution), and the outcome.

### 10. Are you a team player or prefer working independently?

Most companies want both. Say you adapt — you collaborate when brainstorming and problem-solving, and work independently when execution requires focus.

## Conflict and challenge questions

### 11. Describe a conflict with a colleague and how you resolved it

Use STAR. Stay objective, avoid blame, and emphasise what you learned about collaboration.

### 12. Tell me about a time you failed

Choose a genuine failure. Explain what went wrong, what you did immediately to limit the damage, and the lasting lesson you took from it.

### 13. How do you handle feedback and criticism?

Show that you welcome it. Give an example of a time feedback improved your work.

### 14. Describe a situation where you showed leadership

Leadership does not require a title. Organising a hackathon team or mentoring a junior colleague counts.

### 15. Have you ever disagreed with a manager? What did you do?

Show professional assertiveness: you raised your concern with evidence, listened to their perspective, and ultimately supported the team's decision.

## Goals and values

### 16. What are your salary expectations?

Research the market range for the role and location. Give a range, and anchor slightly above your minimum acceptable figure.

### 17. Are you willing to relocate or travel?

Be honest about your constraints. If you have flexibility, say so.

### 18. What is your notice period?

State it clearly. If you can negotiate a shorter period, mention it.

### 19. Do you have any other offers?

You can be honest without revealing specific numbers. Saying "I am in final stages with one other company" is acceptable and can positively signal demand.

### 20. Why are you leaving your current company? (or Why did you choose this company after graduation?)

For freshers: explain your genuine reason for targeting this company over others — role fit, growth opportunity, domain interest.

## Situational and future questions

### 21 to 30 — Rapid preparation checklist

- What does success look like for you in this role at 90 days?
- Describe a time you had to learn something quickly
- How do you prioritise when everything is urgent?
- What kind of manager do you work best with?
- Describe your ideal work environment
- Tell me about a project you are most proud of
- How do you stay updated with industry trends?
- What do you do outside work that makes you better at your job?
- Is there anything in your background you would like to explain?
- Do you have any questions for us?

Always have two or three genuine questions ready for the interviewer. Asking nothing signals low interest.

## Practice tip

Record yourself answering five questions from this list each day. Watching the playback is uncomfortable but transformative. PlacementDo's HR persona gives you a realistic interviewer experience with structured feedback after every session.

title: How to Get the Most Out of Mock Interview Practice
author: PlacementDo Team
excerpt: Mock interviews only work if you treat them like the real thing. Here is a science-backed approach to deliberate practice that accelerates improvement and builds genuine confidence.
content:
# How to Get the Most Out of Mock Interview Practice

Most candidates who do mock interviews improve. Most candidates who do not, do not. But there is a big difference between going through the motions and deliberate practice that genuinely prepares you for a high-stakes interview.

## Why mock interviews work

The research on deliberate practice is clear: performance improves fastest when you practise under realistic conditions, receive immediate feedback, and iterate. Mock interviews create the context pressure (stakes, time limit, evaluator watching) that simple study cannot replicate.

## The single biggest mistake in mock practice

Treating a mock like a safe rehearsal rather than a real test. If you pause to think "let me start that over," you are not practising the skill you actually need. Commit fully to every answer, even the imperfect ones.

## Before the mock: set a specific goal

Do not just "do a mock interview." Set a target for that session:

- "I will use the STAR framework for every behavioural question"
- "I will think aloud for every coding problem"
- "I will ask a clarifying question before starting each answer"

A focused session beats a vague one every time.

## During the mock: behave as if it is real

- Set up in a quiet location
- Dress as you would for an actual interview (this signals your brain that the stakes are real)
- Do not pause to look things up — if you do not know, say so and work around it
- Watch your filler words: "um," "like," and "you know" undermine your credibility

## After the mock: structured debrief

This is where most of the learning happens. Immediately after each session:

1. Write down every question you struggled with
2. For each, identify the root cause: knowledge gap, structural weakness, or anxiety
3. Spend 15 minutes improving just those weak points before the next session

PlacementDo generates a post-session report that scores you on communication clarity, technical accuracy, and response structure. Use that report as your debrief input.

## Cadence recommendation

- Beginner: two to three mocks per week with full debriefs
- Intermediate (one to two weeks before interviews): one mock per day, focus on weak areas
- Final week: one mock every two days; focus shifts to confidence and consistency

## Using different personas

If your mock interviews always use the same style of interviewer, you are practising for one scenario. Rotate between different interview styles — technical deep-dives, behavioural-heavy, and fast-paced screens — so you stay adaptable.

PlacementDo offers six distinct interviewer personas ranging from a supportive coach to a demanding FAANG-style interviewer. Using the full range prepares you for the full spectrum of real interview styles.

## Combining mock interviews with other preparation

Mock interviews are most effective when combined with:

- Targeted reading to fill knowledge gaps identified in debriefs
- Spaced-repetition flashcards for key concepts
- Recording and rewatching your mock sessions once a week

Consistency over two to four weeks of deliberate mock practice produces improvements that single-day cramming sessions cannot match.

title: Aptitude Test Preparation: Topics, Tips, and Practice Strategy
author: PlacementDo Team
excerpt: Most placement seasons are won or lost in the aptitude round. A structured three-week plan covering quant, logical reasoning, and verbal ability will get you through the filter.
content:
# Aptitude Test Preparation: Topics, Tips, and Practice Strategy

The aptitude test is the first elimination round in almost every campus and off-campus placement drive. Scoring well here separates you from the majority and earns you a seat at the technical or interview table. This guide gives you the complete topic list and a three-week preparation plan.

## Section 1 — Quantitative aptitude

Expect 20 to 30 questions in 25 to 40 minutes. Mastery of these topics is non-negotiable:

### Arithmetic
- Percentages and their applications
- Profit, loss, and discount
- Simple and compound interest
- Ratio, proportion, and variation
- Time, speed, and distance
- Time and work, pipes and cisterns

### Number theory and algebra
- HCF, LCM, and divisibility rules
- Surds, indices, and logarithms
- Linear and quadratic equations
- Progressions (AP and GP)

### Geometry and data interpretation
- Mensuration: areas and volumes of common shapes
- Data interpretation: bar charts, pie charts, line graphs, tables

The trick with quant is not memorising formulas — it is recognising which formula applies within 20 seconds of reading the question. Speed comes from pattern recognition, which only comes from volume of practice.

## Section 2 — Logical reasoning

This section tests your ability to find patterns and draw inferences under time pressure.

### Verbal reasoning
- Syllogisms and logical deduction
- Analogies and classifications
- Statement-conclusion and statement-assumption types
- Blood relations
- Direction sense

### Non-verbal and analytical reasoning
- Series completion (number and letter)
- Coding-decoding
- Seating arrangements (linear and circular)
- Puzzles and input-output
- Data sufficiency

## Section 3 — Verbal ability

- Reading comprehension (two to three passages)
- Sentence correction and error spotting
- Para-jumbles and sentence ordering
- Fill in the blanks (vocabulary and grammar)
- Synonyms and antonyms

## Three-week preparation plan

### Week 1 — Foundations

Spend 90 minutes per day covering one topic per session. Do not time yourself yet. Build conceptual clarity first.

- Days 1–2: Arithmetic basics
- Days 3–4: Number theory and algebra
- Days 5–6: Logical reasoning foundations
- Day 7: Verbal comprehension techniques

### Week 2 — Speed building

Now add the clock. Practice 30-question timed sets for each section. Target 80 percent accuracy before moving to the next topic.

- Days 1–3: Quant mixed sets
- Days 4–5: Reasoning mixed sets
- Days 6–7: Verbal mixed sets

### Week 3 — Full mocks

Take at least three full-length mock aptitude tests under exam conditions. Analyse every wrong answer and categorise errors as:

- Concept gap
- Calculation mistake
- Misread question
- Time pressure error

Each error type has a different remedy. Concept gaps need more study; calculation mistakes need more drill; misreads need a slower first pass; time errors need practice on pacing strategy.

## Test-day tips

- Attempt easy questions first to bank marks, then return to hard ones
- Avoid negative guessing unless you can eliminate at least two options
- Keep a mental clock — know your per-question budget going in
- Stay calm: anxiety burns time. A steady pace beats a frantic one every time.

title: TCS NQT and Interview Preparation: What to Expect and How to Crack It
author: PlacementDo Team
excerpt: TCS hires over 40,000 freshers each year through its NQT. This guide breaks down every section of the test and the interview process so you know exactly how to prepare.
content:
# TCS NQT and Interview Preparation: What to Expect and How to Crack It

Tata Consultancy Services is one of the largest recruiters of engineering graduates in India. The TCS National Qualifier Test (NQT) is the standardised gateway to a TCS offer. Understanding its structure and what the interviewers value gives you a clear preparation advantage.

## TCS NQT: test structure overview

The NQT has two main sections:

### Foundation section (mandatory for all)
- Verbal ability: 24 questions, 30 minutes
- Reasoning ability: 30 questions, 50 minutes
- Numerical ability: 26 questions, 40 minutes

### Advanced section (for higher-band roles)
- Advanced quantitative aptitude: 20 questions, 30 minutes
- Advanced reasoning: 20 questions, 30 minutes
- Data interpretation: 10 questions, 20 minutes
- Coding: 2 problems, 60 minutes

The coding section uses a proprietary TCS IDE. You can use C, C++, Java, or Python. Problems are typically at an easy-to-medium difficulty level.

## What TCS looks for

TCS primarily hires for trainee roles where learning agility matters more than deep domain expertise. They look for:

- Strong foundational communication skills
- Basic coding ability and logical thinking
- Positive attitude and adaptability
- Willingness to work in different technology stacks

## Technical interview preparation

Common technical topics in TCS interviews:

- C and C++ basics (pointers, memory management, OOP concepts)
- Data structures: arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees
- DBMS: SQL queries, normalization, ACID properties
- Computer networks: OSI model, TCP/IP, HTTP vs HTTPS
- Operating systems: process scheduling, memory management
- Your final year and academic projects in depth

Know every line of your project. TCS interviewers frequently use the resume and project work as the entire basis for the technical round.

## HR interview at TCS

The TCS HR round is conversational and fairly standard. Expect:

- Tell me about yourself
- Why TCS?
- Are you comfortable with service-based projects, bond periods, and location changes?
- What is your salary expectation?

Be honest about the bond and location questions. TCS interviewers value clarity over evasion.

## Common pitfalls in TCS selection

- Skipping the verbal section: verbal scores filter heavily at the NQT stage
- Not practising code on a limited IDE: TCS's coding environment does not autocomplete
- Poor communication in the HR round: clear, confident English is weighted heavily

## Preparation resources

Practise TCS-style aptitude questions, run mock coding sessions in a plain editor, and do at least two mock HR sessions before the actual interview. PlacementDo's conversational HR persona closely mimics the tone and pacing of a TCS HR interview.

title: Infosys Interview Preparation: InfyTQ, Hackwithinfy, and the Interview Process
author: PlacementDo Team
excerpt: Infosys recruits through InfyTQ certification and Hackwithinfy. This complete guide covers both pathways, the test format, and what the technical and HR panels evaluate.
content:
# Infosys Interview Preparation: InfyTQ, Hackwithinfy, and the Interview Process

Infosys, one of India's largest IT employers, uses two primary recruitment pathways for freshers: InfyTQ certification-based hiring and Hackwithinfy for top coders. Understanding both tracks and the interview process that follows will give you a clear edge.

## Pathway 1 — InfyTQ

InfyTQ is Infosys's free learning and assessment platform. After completing the recommended courses, you take a proficiency test. High scorers are directly invited for the interview, bypassing the normal campus shortlisting.

### InfyTQ test structure
- Aptitude and logical reasoning: 20 questions
- Verbal ability: 20 questions
- Coding: 2 problems (Python-focused, but Java and C++ are supported)

The coding questions are easier than competitive programming but require clean, working solutions with good edge case handling.

## Pathway 2 — Hackwithinfy

Hackwithinfy is Infosys's national coding competition. Top performers across rounds are shortlisted for the Systems Engineer or Power Programmer role directly. The coding problems are harder — expect medium to hard difficulty data structure and algorithm questions.

## The Infosys interview: Technical round

Typically lasts 30 to 45 minutes. Expect questions on:

- Programming fundamentals in your preferred language
- Object-oriented programming: classes, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction
- DBMS: normalization, SQL, transactions
- Data structures and algorithm complexity
- Your academic projects — in significant depth

Infosys interviewers often ask you to write code on paper or in a plain text editor. Practise writing code without IDE assistance.

## The Infosys HR round

The HR round at Infosys typically covers:

- Introduction and background
- Why Infosys?
- Willingness to relocate and work in any technology
- Questions about your strengths, weaknesses, and a past challenge
- Salary expectations and notice period

Be ready to articulate clearly why you want to join Infosys specifically, not just IT in general. Reference their focus on digital transformation, sustainability initiatives, or specific service areas you find genuinely interesting.

## Study plan for Infosys

- Week 1: Complete InfyTQ recommended courses, cover OOP and DBMS fundamentals
- Week 2: Daily coding practice (two to three problems), mock aptitude tests
- Week 3: Mock technical and HR interviews; research Infosys's recent news and projects

Run at least two full mock interview sessions before the actual panel. PlacementDo offers HR and technical interview simulations that prepare you for the specific conversational style Infosys interviewers use.

title: 50 Data Structures and Algorithms Interview Questions for Placement
author: PlacementDo Team
excerpt: From arrays and linked lists to graphs and dynamic programming, these are the 50 most-tested DSA questions across TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, and product company campus drives.
content:
# 50 Data Structures and Algorithms Interview Questions for Placement

Data structures and algorithms form the foundation of every software engineering technical interview. This curated list of 50 questions covers the topics most frequently tested across campus placement drives, IT services companies, and product start-ups.

## Arrays and strings (questions 1–10)

1. Find the maximum subarray sum (Kadane's algorithm)
2. Rotate an array by K positions
3. Find all pairs in an array that sum to a target value
4. Find the first non-repeating character in a string
5. Check if a string is an anagram of another
6. Merge two sorted arrays in O(1) extra space
7. Move all zeroes to the end of an array without changing relative order
8. Find the longest common prefix among a list of strings
9. Implement strStr (find a substring in a string)
10. Count the frequency of each character in a string

## Linked lists (questions 11–18)

11. Reverse a linked list iteratively and recursively
12. Detect a cycle in a linked list (Floyd's algorithm)
13. Find the middle node of a linked list in one pass
14. Merge two sorted linked lists
15. Remove the Nth node from the end of a list
16. Add two numbers represented as linked lists
17. Flatten a multilevel doubly linked list
18. Clone a linked list with a next and random pointer

## Stacks and queues (questions 19–24)

19. Implement a stack using two queues
20. Evaluate a postfix expression
21. Find the largest rectangle in a histogram
22. Implement a queue using two stacks
23. Next greater element for every array element
24. Minimum stack: design a stack that retrieves the minimum in O(1)

## Trees and binary search trees (questions 25–33)

25. Level-order traversal of a binary tree
26. Check if a binary tree is height-balanced
27. Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes
28. Serialize and deserialize a binary tree
29. Validate a binary search tree
30. Find the Kth smallest element in a BST
31. Convert a sorted array to a balanced BST
32. Diameter of a binary tree
33. Right side view of a binary tree

## Graphs (questions 34–40)

34. BFS and DFS implementation with adjacency list
35. Detect a cycle in a directed graph
36. Topological sort of a DAG
37. Find all connected components in an undirected graph
38. Shortest path in an unweighted graph (BFS)
39. Number of islands (2D grid BFS/DFS)
40. Check if a graph is bipartite

## Hashing (questions 41–44)

41. Find the first duplicate element in an array
42. Longest consecutive sequence in an unsorted array
43. Group anagrams together from a list of strings
44. Two-sum using a hashmap in O(n)

## Dynamic programming (questions 45–50)

45. Fibonacci number using memoization and bottom-up DP
46. 0/1 knapsack problem
47. Longest common subsequence
48. Coin change problem (minimum coins)
49. Longest increasing subsequence
50. Edit distance between two strings

## How to approach DSA questions in interviews

When given a coding problem in an interview:

- Ask one or two clarifying questions about constraints and edge cases
- State your brute-force approach first, then identify the optimisation
- Write pseudocode before actual code if the problem is complex
- Think out loud throughout — interviewers score the process, not just the answer
- Always discuss time and space complexity at the end

Practise at least ten problems from each category above. Track your solve times and revisit problems you could not solve within 25 minutes. Consistent daily practice over four to six weeks is the most reliable path to interview-day confidence.

title: Career Guidance for Engineering Graduates: How to Choose Your First Job
author: PlacementDo Team
excerpt: Your first job sets the trajectory for the next decade. Here is a practical framework for evaluating offers, understanding the IT versus product company trade-off, and making a decision you will be proud of.
content:
# Career Guidance for Engineering Graduates: How to Choose Your First Job

Getting your first job offer is exciting. Getting the right first job takes a little more thought. The decisions you make in your first two years shape which doors open in your late twenties. This guide gives you a clear framework for evaluating offers and building a career with intention.

## The service company vs. product company trade-off

Most engineering graduates face a choice between IT services companies and product companies. Neither is objectively better — they offer different experiences.

### IT services companies (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture)

Advantages:
- Stable employment with structured training programmes
- Broad technology exposure across different clients and domains
- Lower risk and a reliable first paycheck
- Large alumni networks that are useful later

Considerations:
- Work is often maintenance or support-heavy rather than greenfield development
- Growth speed depends heavily on which project you land on
- Switching to product companies later requires deliberate upskilling

### Product companies and start-ups

Advantages:
- Closer to the full software development lifecycle
- Faster ownership and responsibility growth
- More aligned to what product company interviewers look for

Considerations:
- Higher risk, especially at early-stage start-ups
- Less structured onboarding for freshers
- Compensation varies widely

## How to evaluate a job offer

When comparing offers, look beyond the CTC figure:

### Learning opportunity
Is the role technically challenging? Will you build skills that are in demand two years from now? A lower-paid role with strong technical mentorship is often more valuable early in your career than a higher CTC in a maintenance role.

### Domain and technology stack
Are you excited about the product or domain? Enthusiasm translates to faster learning and better performance reviews.

### Growth path
Ask the interviewer: what does a successful person in this role look like at one year and three years? The quality of the answer tells you a lot about how structured career development is.

### Location and work model
Remote, hybrid, or in-office? Factor in real cost of living, commute, and your personal preferences. A 15 percent salary premium may be entirely consumed by living costs in a more expensive city.

### Company stability
Check the company's funding status (for start-ups), revenue trend, and Glassdoor reviews with a critical eye. For IT services companies, check bench rates and attrition.

## Building your first two years intentionally

Your first job is also your first reputation. A few principles:

- Volunteer for the hardest projects, not the easiest ones
- Find a mentor inside or outside your team within the first three months
- Build one side project each year that demonstrates skills beyond your day job
- Track your achievements monthly so you always have resume material ready

## When to consider switching

The average software engineer in India switches roles every 18 to 24 months. Switching is healthy if you are moving toward better learning, better compensation, or a more interesting domain. Switch away from stagnation, not just for a salary bump alone.

Prepare for your next move before you need it. Keep your skills current, maintain your network, and practise interviews regularly — not just when you are desperate. PlacementDo is built for exactly this: keeping your interview skills sharp so you are always ready when an opportunity appears.

# Technical Interview Tips for Software Engineers: From Screening to Offer

A technical interview is not purely a test of what you know. It is an evaluation of how you think, communicate, and collaborate under pressure. Many candidates with strong knowledge underperform because they focus entirely on getting the right answer and neglect the process of getting there. This guide gives you the strategies that work across all stages of a technical interview.

## The phone or video screen

The screening round is designed to filter out candidates who are fundamentally unprepared. Keep it simple:

- Have your resume open in front of you — references are expected
- Speak slowly and clearly; phone audio is forgiving of content, not of muddled delivery
- Expect one or two straightforward DSA questions at easy difficulty
- If you are stuck, say what you know and what you would look up — never fake knowledge

## System design rounds (for experienced candidates)

If you are interviewing for a mid-level or senior role, system design rounds test your ability to architect scalable systems. Key principles:

- Clarify requirements and constraints before designing anything
- Start with a high-level architecture, then drill into components the interviewer asks about
- Discuss trade-offs explicitly: SQL vs. NoSQL, synchronous vs. asynchronous processing, monolith vs. microservices
- Acknowledge what you do not know rather than guessing with false confidence

## Coding round best practices

### Before you code
- Restate the problem in your own words to confirm understanding
- Ask about constraints: input size, null handling, edge cases
- State your approach before writing a single line

### While you code
- Write clean, readable code over clever one-liners
- Name variables clearly: `maxProfit` beats `mp`
- Comment complex logic briefly
- If you get stuck, work through a small concrete example on paper or the whiteboard

### After you code
- Walk through your solution with the sample input
- Identify any edge cases you might have missed
- State the time and space complexity and explain why

## Handling questions you do not know

This is where many candidates lose marks unnecessarily. The right response is:

1. Acknowledge that you are not immediately sure
2. Reason out loud from first principles toward a plausible answer
3. If you genuinely cannot find a path, ask for a hint and say you would look it up in practice

Interviewers respect intellectual honesty. They do not respect guessing presented as fact.

## After the interview: what to do immediately

- Send a brief thank-you note within 24 hours
- Write down every question you were asked — this is valuable preparation data
- Identify the gaps in your knowledge revealed by the interview and fill them before the next round

## The mindset shift that changes everything

Stop thinking of technical interviews as pass/fail tests. Think of them as collaborative problem-solving sessions with an experienced engineer. Your job is to show how you would be to work with on a daily basis — curious, methodical, honest, and clear. That mindset shift changes how you communicate, ask questions, and respond to feedback, and it is the single most impactful change most candidates can make.

Read quality English news sources daily for two weeks before the test — it improves vocabulary and argument structure naturally.

# What Is Placement? Complete Guide to Campus Placement in India 2026

If you are a college student in India, you have almost certainly heard the word placement dozens of times. But what does placement actually mean, how does the process work, and what separates students who get placed from those who do not? This guide answers every fundamental question about placement and gives you a concrete starting point for your preparation.

## What Is Placement?

Placement — in the context of higher education in India — refers to the process by which companies recruit students directly from college campuses before or immediately after graduation. When a student gets placed, they receive a formal job offer from a company, often before they have even completed their degree.

The term is used broadly to refer to both campus placement (companies visiting your college) and off-campus placement (applying directly to companies outside the college recruitment process).

## How Does Campus Placement Work?

Every college has a Training and Placement Cell (T&P Cell) that coordinates with companies to schedule recruitment drives. Here is the typical flow:

### Step 1: Company Registration and Announcement
The T&P Cell invites companies and announces the schedule to students. You register for companies you want to apply to.

### Step 2: Pre-Placement Talk (PPT)
Companies often hold a presentation explaining their culture, roles, packages, and expectations. Attend these — they reveal what the company values.

### Step 3: Aptitude Test
The online or written test filters candidates. This typically covers quantitative aptitude, logical reasoning, verbal ability, and sometimes a coding section.

### Step 4: Technical Rounds
Candidates who clear the test go through one or more technical interviews. These assess coding ability, CS fundamentals, and project knowledge.

### Step 5: HR Round
The final round assesses communication, attitude, and cultural fit. Questions cover your background, goals, and behavioural scenarios.

### Step 6: Offer Letter
Successful candidates receive an offer letter with role, salary, joining date, and other terms.

## Types of Placement

### On-Campus Placement
Companies visit your college campus. The T&P Cell manages the process. This is the most common route for engineering and MBA freshers.

### Off-Campus Placement
You apply directly to companies through their careers page or job portals like LinkedIn, Naukri, or Internshala. No T&P Cell involvement. Requires proactive outreach.

### Pool Campus Placement
Multiple colleges pool students for a single company drive at one location. Common for tier-2 and tier-3 engineering colleges.

### Lateral Placement
For candidates with 1–3 years of work experience moving to a new company. Different process from campus placement.

## What Do Companies Look for in Placement?

Companies hiring through campus placement primarily evaluate:

- **Academic performance**: Most companies have minimum CGPA cutoffs (typically 6.0–7.5)
- **Aptitude and reasoning**: Speed and accuracy in quantitative and verbal sections
- **Technical knowledge**: DSA, CS fundamentals, language proficiency
- **Communication**: Clarity, confidence, and structure in verbal responses
- **Attitude and culture fit**: Enthusiasm, adaptability, and professionalism

## How to Improve Your Placement Chances

### Maintain a Strong CGPA
Most top placement companies have CGPA cutoffs. Aim for above 7.0 consistently.

### Build Real Projects
Two or three genuinely interesting projects that you built yourself matter more than a resume full of generic coursework.

### Practise Aptitude Consistently
The aptitude test is the biggest filter. 30 minutes daily for 2–3 months makes a measurable difference.

### Do AI Mock Interviews
Practising out loud with structured feedback — like PlacementDo's AI mock interview platform — builds confidence and catches communication gaps before they cost you an offer.

### Research Target Companies
Know the company's products, culture, and recent news. Candidates who show genuine interest stand out in HR rounds.

## Placement Statistics in India (2026)

- Over 3 million engineering graduates enter the job market annually
- Average campus placement rate at IITs: 85–90%
- Average campus placement rate at NITs: 60–75%
- Average campus placement rate at private engineering colleges: 30–50%
- Top IT service companies hire 30,000–50,000 freshers per year

## FAQ: Campus Placement in India

### Q: What is a good placement package for freshers in 2026?
A: Service companies offer 3–5 LPA. Product startups offer 6–15 LPA. FAANG companies offer 20–40+ LPA for top performers.

### Q: Can I participate in placement with an active backlog?
A: Most companies have a no-backlog requirement at the time of joining. Some allow participation if the backlog will be cleared before joining.

### Q: What happens if I do not get placed in campus recruitment?
A: Off-campus applications, referrals, internship extensions, and coding competitions are all valid alternative routes. Off-campus placement is increasingly common and effective.

# 50 HR Interview Questions for Freshers with Best Answers (2026)

The HR round in campus placement is often underestimated by freshers who focus all their energy on aptitude and technical preparation. This is a costly mistake — HR rounds eliminate 20–30% of candidates who cleared technical stages. These 50 questions cover everything an HR interviewer will ask during your placement process.

## Questions 1–10: About Yourself and Background

### 1. Tell me about yourself.
Structure: 90 seconds. Education → key project or achievement → core strengths → what you are looking for. End with enthusiasm for the role.

### 2. Walk me through your resume.
Highlight the 2–3 most relevant experiences for this role. Show logical progression, not just chronology.

### 3. What are your greatest strengths?
Pick two specific strengths with evidence. Example: "My strongest skill is breaking complex problems into smaller steps — I used this to debug a 3-week-stuck performance issue in my final year project."

### 4. What is your biggest weakness?
Choose a real weakness not critical to the role. Describe your specific action plan to address it. Show progress.

### 5. Why should we hire you?
Link your specific skills directly to the job requirements. End with genuine enthusiasm.

### 6. Where do you see yourself in 5 years?
Show ambition aligned with the career path this company offers. Avoid vague answers like "senior role" — be specific about the skill growth you want.

### 7. What motivates you?
Give a genuine answer — problem-solving, impact, learning, collaboration. Back it with a real example.

### 8. Describe yourself in 3 words.
Choose words you can back with evidence: analytical, consistent, curious.

### 9. What are your hobbies?
Mention activities that demonstrate useful traits — coding competitions (persistence), reading (curiosity), sports (teamwork).

### 10. Are you a leader or a follower?
Say you adapt: you lead when the situation needs direction, follow when others have more expertise.

## Questions 11–20: Motivation and Company Fit

### 11. Why do you want to work at this company?
Research specifically: recent products, culture values, growth trajectory. Reference something real.

### 12. Why did you choose your field of study?
Give your genuine reason, not a rehearsed answer. Authenticity matters here.

### 13. What do you know about our company?
Mention: founders/history, primary products/services, recent news, company values. Show you prepared.

### 14. Why do you want this specific role?
Map 2–3 of your skills to the role requirements. Show role-fit, not just company-fit.

### 15. Are you comfortable with relocation?
Be honest about constraints. If flexible, say so explicitly.

### 16. Are you comfortable with night shifts or rotational shifts?
Be honest. Avoid saying yes and planning to say no after joining.

### 17. What is your expected salary?
Research market rates for the role and location. Give a range anchored slightly above your minimum.

### 18. Do you have any other offers or ongoing interviews?
You can be honest without revealing specifics. "I am in final stages with one other company" is acceptable.

### 19. When can you join?
State your actual availability honestly.

### 20. Are you willing to sign a service bond?
Be honest about your intentions. If you are comfortable, say so. If not, say you would like to understand the terms.

## Questions 21–30: Behavioural and Situational

### 21. Describe a time you worked in a team.
Use STAR. Focus on your specific contribution and how you handled a team dynamic challenge.

### 22. Tell me about a time you failed.
Choose a genuine failure. Explain immediate response, long-term lesson, behaviour change.

### 23. Describe a conflict with a colleague and how you resolved it.
Stay objective, avoid blame, show empathy and communication.

### 24. Give an example of when you showed leadership.
Leadership without a title counts: organising a hackathon team, mentoring a junior, driving a group project.

### 25. Describe a time you handled criticism.
Show that you welcome feedback and act on it specifically.

### 26. Tell me about a time you worked under pressure.
Describe the situation, your prioritisation strategy, and the outcome.

### 27. Give an example of a goal you set and achieved.
Be specific with the goal, timeline, and measurable outcome.

### 28. Describe a situation where you took initiative.
Show that you do not wait to be told. Initiative without being asked is a top hiring signal.

### 29. How do you handle multiple tasks with competing deadlines?
Describe your actual prioritisation method: urgency vs. importance matrix, daily planning, stakeholder communication.

### 30. Tell me about your most challenging academic project.
Focus on what made it hard, how you approached the challenge, and what you learned.

## Questions 31–50: Rapid Preparation Checklist

31. What type of work environment do you prefer?
32. What do you do outside academics that makes you better at your work?
33. How do you stay current with technology trends?
34. What is your approach to learning new skills?
35. Are you comfortable working independently?
36. What kind of manager do you work best with?
37. How do you handle failure and setbacks?
38. What would your professors say about you?
39. Tell me about a time you had to adapt quickly to a change.
40. How do you approach a task you have never done before?
41. What is success for you in this role at 90 days?
42. Describe a project you are most proud of.
43. Do you prefer working on one project or multiple?
44. How do you communicate with team members who have different working styles?
45. What would you do if you disagreed with your manager?
46. Have you ever made a mistake at work or in a project? How did you handle it?
47. What do you bring to the team that others might not?
48. Are you open to feedback from peers, not just managers?
49. Is there anything in your background you would like to explain?
50. Do you have any questions for us? (Always prepare 2–3 genuine questions)

## FAQ: HR Interview for Placement

### Q: How long is a typical HR round in campus placement?
A: 15–30 minutes for most service companies. Product companies may run longer HR interviews (45–60 min).

### Q: Should I memorise answers for HR interviews?
A: No — memorised answers sound rehearsed and inauthentic. Prepare structures and key points, then speak naturally.

### Q: What is the most important HR interview question for freshers?
A: Tell me about yourself. It sets the entire tone. Practise this one until it feels natural and confident.

# Accenture Placement Preparation 2026: Test Pattern, Questions and Interview Tips

Accenture is one of the largest global IT services companies and among the biggest campus recruiters in India, hiring thousands of freshers annually. Getting placed at Accenture is achievable with focused preparation — this guide covers everything you need to know.

## Accenture Recruitment Process Overview

Accenture's campus placement process has three main stages:

### Stage 1: Cognitive and Technical Assessment (CTA)
- Cognitive ability: 50 questions, 70 minutes
- Technical (IT domain): 40 questions, 40 minutes
- Cognitive covers: verbal reasoning, attention to detail, abstract reasoning
- Technical covers: programming concepts, DBMS basics, networking, data structures

### Stage 2: Communication Assessment
This is Accenture-specific and tests English communication skills:
- Multitasking skills: listening with simultaneous reading
- Essay writing on a given topic (20 minutes)
- Spoken English evaluation (recorded responses)

### Stage 3: Interview Round
- Technical + HR combined (30–45 minutes)
- Conversational style — less formal than product companies
- Focus on projects, CS fundamentals, and communication clarity

## Cognitive Assessment Syllabus

### Verbal Reasoning
- Reading comprehension
- Sentence completion and correction
- Analogies and classifications
- Critical reasoning

### Attention to Detail
- Spot the difference in data tables
- Proofreading tasks
- Sequential instructions comprehension

### Abstract Reasoning
- Pattern recognition in shapes
- Matrix completion
- Next in series

## Technical Assessment Syllabus

- Programming fundamentals (C, Java, Python)
- Data structures: arrays, linked lists, trees
- DBMS: SQL, normalization, joins
- Computer networks: OSI model, TCP/IP, HTTP
- Operating systems: process management, scheduling
- Output prediction and code debugging

## Communication Assessment Tips

### Essay Writing (20 minutes)
Structure: Introduction (2 sentences), Body (3 supporting points), Conclusion (1–2 sentences). Write coherent prose — not bullet points. Focus on clarity over complexity.

### Multitasking Task
Practise reading a passage while simultaneously listening to different content. This tests divided attention, not knowledge.

## Interview Round Preparation

Accenture interviewers are typically less intimidating than product company panels. They focus on:
- Your academic background and projects
- Basic programming and CS concepts
- Communication clarity
- Why Accenture? What do you know about the company?
- Are you comfortable with service-based projects and client work?

## 2-Week Accenture Preparation Plan

### Week 1
- Days 1–2: Complete verbal reasoning topic practice
- Days 3–4: Technical MCQ practice (DBMS + OS + networks)
- Days 5–6: Essay writing practice (1 essay daily on a general topic)
- Day 7: Full mock test (CTA simulation)

### Week 2
- Days 1–3: Attention to detail and abstract reasoning practice
- Days 4–5: Communication assessment practice
- Days 6–7: Mock interview sessions — technical + HR

## FAQ: Accenture Placement

### Q: What is Accenture's package for freshers in 2026?
A: Accenture offers approximately 4.5–7 LPA for ASE (Application Software Engineering) roles at campus. Higher packages are available for specialist tracks.

### Q: Does Accenture ask DSA coding problems?
A: The placement test has programming MCQs, not live coding. The technical interview may include basic algorithmic questions but rarely complex DSA.

### Q: Is Accenture a good first company for freshers?
A: Yes — Accenture provides structured training, large alumni network, exposure to global clients, and a stable entry-level career. It is an excellent placement for freshers targeting IT services.

# Cognizant GenC Placement Guide 2026: Pattern, Syllabus and Interview Tips

Cognizant Technology Solutions is among India's top 5 IT employers and recruits tens of thousands of freshers annually through its GenC (Generate Commerce) programme. There are two tracks: GenC (general) and GenC Next (for stronger coders at higher packages). This guide covers both.

## Cognizant Recruitment Tracks

### GenC (Standard Track)
- Package: ~4 LPA
- Roles: Junior software engineering, testing, and support
- Assessment: eSEAT (online test) + HR interview

### GenC Next (Premium Track)
- Package: ~6.5 LPA and above
- Roles: Software development, digital engineering
- Assessment: eSEAT + Technical interview + HR interview
- Requires stronger coding ability

## Cognizant eSEAT Test Pattern

The Employability Skills English Aptitude Test (eSEAT) consists of:

### Aptitude Section (75 minutes)
- Quantitative aptitude: 25 questions
- Logical reasoning: 15 questions
- Verbal ability: 25 questions

### Coding Section (GenC Next only, 45 minutes)
- 2 programming problems
- Easy to medium DSA difficulty
- Python, Java, C, or C++ supported

## Aptitude Syllabus

### Quantitative
- Number system and divisibility
- Percentages and profit-loss
- Time-speed-distance and work-time
- Averages and mixtures
- Permutations and combinations
- Data interpretation

### Logical Reasoning
- Seating arrangement
- Blood relations
- Syllogisms
- Coding-decoding
- Direction and distance

### Verbal Ability
- Reading comprehension (2 passages)
- Sentence correction and error identification
- Synonyms and antonyms
- Fill in the blanks

## Technical Interview (GenC Next)

Focused 30–45 minute session covering:
- OOP concepts in your preferred language
- Data structures and algorithm basics
- DBMS: SQL queries, joins, normalization
- OS fundamentals
- Your academic projects in depth
- 1–2 simple coding problems on paper/whiteboard

## HR Interview

Cognizant HR rounds are conversational and positive. Key topics:
- Tell me about yourself (this matters more than you think)
- Why Cognizant?
- Flexibility with location, technology, and project type
- Salary expectations
- Future goals

## 3-Week Cognizant Preparation Plan

### Week 1: Aptitude Strong Foundation
- Daily 45-minute quant + reasoning practice
- Focus on speed — the eSEAT is time-pressured

### Week 2: Verbal + Coding (GenC Next)
- Reading comprehension timed practice
- 2–3 easy LeetCode problems daily
- One full eSEAT mock test by end of week

### Week 3: Interview Preparation
- Mock technical interview (OOP, DBMS, projects)
- HR question preparation — answer out loud
- Company research: Cognizant's key clients, recent news, culture

## FAQ: Cognizant Placement

### Q: What is the difference between GenC and GenC Next?
A: GenC is the standard hire track. GenC Next is for stronger technical candidates with higher starting packages and more challenging roles. Both participate in the same eSEAT but Next has an additional coding section.

### Q: Does Cognizant visit all engineering colleges?
A: Cognizant visits most mid-to-large engineering colleges with placement drive MoUs. They also conduct large off-campus pools. Check the CTS careers portal regularly.

title: Top 30 Aptitude Shortcuts and Tricks for Placement Tests (With Examples)
author: PlacementDo Team

content:
# Top 30 Aptitude Shortcuts and Tricks for Placement Tests (With Examples)

In a placement aptitude test, speed is as important as accuracy. Most tests allow only 60–90 seconds per question. These 30 shortcuts will help you solve common question types in 15–25 seconds instead of a minute or more.

## Percentage Shortcuts

### Shortcut 1: Percentage Change Formula
Instead of computing base → new → percentage, use: % change = (difference ÷ original) × 100

Example: Price rises from 80 to 100. % change = (20 ÷ 80) × 100 = 25%

### Shortcut 2: Successive Percentage Changes
If a value changes by A% and then B%, net change = A + B + (AB/100)

Example: 20% increase then 10% increase = 20 + 10 + (20×10/100) = 32% net increase

### Shortcut 3: Percentage to Fraction Conversions (Memorise These)
- 10% = 1/10, 12.5% = 1/8, 16.67% = 1/6
- 25% = 1/4, 33.33% = 1/3, 50% = 1/2
- 75% = 3/4, 20% = 1/5, 40% = 2/5

## Ratio and Proportion Shortcuts

### Shortcut 4: Componendo-Dividendo
If a/b = c/d, then (a+b)/(a-b) = (c+d)/(c-d). Useful for ratio comparison problems.

### Shortcut 5: Ratio Comparison Without Common Denominator
To compare a/b vs c/d: compare a×d vs b×c. Larger product = larger ratio.

## Time, Speed, and Distance Shortcuts

### Shortcut 6: Average Speed for Equal Distances
If you travel distance D at speed S1 and return at S2, average speed = 2S1S2/(S1+S2)

Never add and divide — this is the most common mistake in placement exams.

### Shortcut 7: Relative Speed
- Same direction: relative speed = |S1 – S2|
- Opposite direction: relative speed = S1 + S2

### Shortcut 8: Train Problems
Time for a train of length L to cross a stationary object of length l = (L + l) / speed. For a point object, l = 0.

### Shortcut 9: Time to Cross Another Train
Time = (L1 + L2) / (S1 + S2 if opposite, S1 – S2 if same direction)

## Time and Work Shortcuts

### Shortcut 10: Work Rate Formula
If A does work in 'a' days and B in 'b' days, together they finish in ab/(a+b) days.

### Shortcut 11: Efficiency Method
Assume total work = LCM of individual times. Each person's daily rate = total work ÷ their days. Add rates for combined work.

### Shortcut 12: Work Done in N Days
Work done = N × (combined daily rate). Remaining work = Total – Work done.

## Number System Shortcuts

### Shortcut 13: Divisibility Rules (Memorise)
- Div by 3: sum of digits divisible by 3
- Div by 4: last 2 digits divisible by 4
- Div by 8: last 3 digits divisible by 8
- Div by 9: sum of digits divisible by 9
- Div by 11: alternating sum divisible by 11

### Shortcut 14: Unit Digit Cycles
- 2: 2, 4, 8, 6 (cycle of 4)
- 3: 3, 9, 7, 1 (cycle of 4)
- 7: 7, 9, 3, 1 (cycle of 4)
- 4 and 9: cycle of 2 (4,6 and 9,1)
- 5 and 1: always 5 and 1

Useful for: What is the unit digit of 7^63? Power 63 = 4×15+3, so unit digit = 3rd in cycle = 3.

### Shortcut 15: HCF and LCM Relationship
For any two numbers a and b: HCF × LCM = a × b.

## Profit and Loss Shortcuts

### Shortcut 16: Selling Price Formula
SP = CP × (100 + profit%) / 100 or CP × (100 – loss%) / 100

### Shortcut 17: CP from SP and Profit%
CP = SP × 100 / (100 + profit%)

### Shortcut 18: Dishonest Shopkeeper Problems
If a shopkeeper declares X% profit but uses faulty weights measuring (actual – shortage)g as (actual)g: True profit% = (declared% × actual + shortage × 100) / (actual – shortage)

## Simple and Compound Interest Shortcuts

### Shortcut 19: Simple Interest
SI = PRT/100 where P = principal, R = rate%, T = time in years

### Shortcut 20: Compound Interest (Annual)
CI = P(1 + R/100)^T – P. For small rates and short durations, CI ≈ SI + SI²/P.

### Shortcut 21: Difference Between CI and SI (2 years)
Difference = P×(R/100)²

## Mixtures and Alligation

### Shortcut 22: Alligation Rule
To mix two items of prices A and B to get price C: ratio = (B-C):(C-A)

## Permutations and Combinations

### Shortcut 23: Circular Arrangements
Arranging n people in a circle = (n-1)! not n!

### Shortcut 24: Arrangements with Identical Items
n items with a identical and b identical: arrangements = n! / (a! × b!)

## Data Interpretation Shortcuts

### Shortcut 25: Quick % Calculation in DI
For X% of Y: 10% of Y = Y/10. Then build up. Example: 35% of 840 = 84×3 + 42 = 252 + 42 = 294.

### Shortcut 26: Growth Rate in DI
If value goes from V1 to V2, growth = (V2-V1)/V1 × 100. Do this mentally by finding the difference.

## Logical Reasoning Shortcuts

### Shortcut 27: Venn Diagram (3 sets)
Total = A + B + C – (A∩B) – (B∩C) – (A∩C) + (A∩B∩C)

### Shortcut 28: Calendar Problems
Odd days pattern: January=3, Feb=0(non-leap)/1(leap), March=3, April=2, May=3, June=2, July=3, Aug=3, Sep=2, Oct=3, Nov=2, Dec=3.

## General Exam Strategy

### Shortcut 29: First-Pass Strategy
Attempt all easy questions first (30 seconds each). Mark difficult ones and return if time allows. Never spend more than 90 seconds on one question.

### Shortcut 30: Elimination Before Guessing
Before guessing, eliminate at least 2 options using logical reasoning. This raises your probability from 25% to 50%.

## FAQ: Aptitude Shortcuts for Placement

### Q: How many shortcuts should I memorise for placement tests?
A: Focus on the 10–15 most frequently tested topics for your target companies. Quality of recall under time pressure matters more than quantity memorised.

### Q: Do all placement tests have negative marking?
A: Not all. TCS NQT has no negative marking in foundation; Wipro does not officially confirm. Always check the specific test guidelines before attempting.

content:
# Resume Building Tips for Freshers: Create a Placement-Ready CV in 2026

Your resume is the first thing a recruiter sees — and for campus placement, it shapes every question in the technical and HR round. A strong resume does not just list what you did; it tells a story that makes a recruiter want to interview you. Here is how to build one.

## The Non-Negotiable Rule: One Page

For campus placement, your resume must be one page. No exceptions. Recruiters processing hundreds of resumes per day make split-second decisions. A second page signals poor prioritisation, not more experience.

## Ideal Resume Structure for Freshers

1. Contact Information
2. Professional Summary (optional but powerful)
3. Education
4. Technical Skills
5. Projects (most important for freshers)
6. Internship / Work Experience (if any)
7. Certifications and Awards

## Contact Information

- Full name (large, top of page)
- Professional email: firstname.lastname@gmail.com
- Phone number
- LinkedIn URL (customised: linkedin.com/in/yourname)
- GitHub URL (if your code is public and presentable)
- Location: City, State only — no full address

## Professional Summary

3 lines answering: who you are, what you can do, what you want.

Example: "Final year Computer Science student at XYZ University with strong DSA fundamentals and experience building full-stack applications. Completed a 3-month internship at ABC Startup where I improved backend API response time by 35%. Seeking a software engineering role where I can build scalable products that serve real users."

## Education Section

- Degree, Branch, University, Year of passing, CGPA/Percentage
- Include only if CGPA is above 6.0 or percentage above 60%
- Add relevant coursework if space allows and it is directly relevant

## Technical Skills (Be Honest)

Group by category:
- Programming Languages: Python, Java, C++
- Frameworks: React, Node.js, Spring Boot
- Databases: MySQL, MongoDB
- Tools: Git, Docker, AWS basics
- Concepts: Data Structures, OOP, REST APIs

Never list a skill you cannot defend in a 5-minute technical conversation.

## Projects (Make or Break Section)

This is the most important section for freshers without work experience. For each project:

### Structure Each Project As:
- Project Name + tech stack used
- What it does (1 sentence)
- Your specific contribution (not the team's — yours)
- Quantified outcome: "Reduced loading time by 40%" not "Improved performance"
- GitHub link or live demo link

### Quality Over Quantity
Three strong, well-described projects beat eight vague bullet-point entries. Recruiters ask about every project you list — only include ones you can discuss for 5–10 minutes.

## ATS Optimisation for Placement

Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) filter resumes before a human ever sees them. To pass ATS:
- Use standard section headings (Education, Experience, Skills — not Creative alternatives)
- Include keywords from the job description naturally
- No tables, columns, or graphics (they confuse ATS parsers)
- Submit as PDF unless the job posting specifies Word
- Use a clean, readable font: Calibri, Arial, or Georgia at 10–11pt

## Common Fresher Resume Mistakes

- Listing "MS Office" and "Teamwork" as skills in 2026
- Generic objective: "Seeking an opportunity to utilise my skills in a reputed organisation"
- Copying project descriptions from the internet verbatim
- Using a photo (not required in India for most tech companies — takes space unnecessarily)
- Inconsistent dates, fonts, or formatting
- No quantification: "Built a web app" instead of "Built a web app serving 500+ daily users"

## Final Checklist Before Submitting

- Is it one page?
- Is everything grammatically correct?
- Are all links working?
- Is the CGPA above the company's cutoff?
- Did you tailor the summary for this specific role?
- Can you talk about every single item for at least 2 minutes?

## FAQ: Resume for Placement

### Q: Should I use a resume template from Canva or Zety?
A: Avoid templates with heavy graphics, columns, or tables — they often fail ATS. Use a clean, minimal template or build your own in Google Docs/MS Word.

### Q: How do I write projects if I only built tutorial projects?
A: Extend a tutorial project: add a feature, integrate an API, deploy it, and measure something. Then that becomes a real project worth documenting.

### Q: Should my resume include my class 10 and 12 results?
A: Only if they are above 80% and relevant to the application. If your CGPA is strong, class 10/12 details take up valuable space better used for projects.

title: 10 Common Placement Interview Mistakes Freshers Make (and How to Fix Them)
author: PlacementDo Team

content:
# 10 Common Placement Interview Mistakes Freshers Make (and How to Fix Them)

Placement interviews are competitive. Even technically strong candidates fall at the interview stage due to avoidable mistakes. These 10 errors are the most common reasons freshers fail placement interviews — with exact fixes for each.

## Mistake 1: Not Practising Out Loud

Most freshers prepare their answers in their head. But the interview is a spoken performance. Mental preparation and spoken performance are entirely different skills.

Fix: Practise every answer verbally — record yourself, or use PlacementDo's AI mock interview to get immediate feedback on your spoken delivery.

## Mistake 2: Giving Vague Answers Without Evidence

"I am a good team player" and "I am hardworking" mean nothing without evidence. HR interviewers hear these claims hundreds of times per day.

Fix: Use the STAR framework (Situation, Task, Action, Result) for every behavioural question. Every claim must end with a specific outcome.

## Mistake 3: Not Researching the Company

Freshers frequently cannot answer "Why do you want to work here?" beyond "it is a great company." This signals zero effort.

Fix: Research the company's products, recent news, culture values, and growth trajectory before every interview. Mention something specific and genuine.

## Mistake 4: Listing Skills on the Resume That Cannot be Defended

If your resume says you know Python and the interviewer asks you to explain list comprehensions or decorators, you cannot freeze.

Fix: Only list skills you can discuss for at least 5 minutes under interview pressure. Remove anything you added optimistically.

## Mistake 5: Panicking When Faced With Unknown Questions

Candidates often give wrong guesses or freeze completely when they do not know an answer.

Fix: Say "I am not immediately certain, but let me reason through this." Then think out loud. Interviewers respect intellectual honesty and logical process far more than confident wrong answers.

## Mistake 6: Giving Memorised-Sounding Answers

Questions like "Tell me about yourself" often produce robotic recitations of the resume. Interviewers can tell instantly.

Fix: Prepare a structure, not a script. Know your 3 key points and the order, but speak naturally within that structure each time.

## Mistake 7: Not Asking Any Questions at the End

"Do you have any questions for us?" is not a formality. Saying "No, I do not have any questions" signals disinterest.

Fix: Prepare 3 genuine questions: about the team, about the onboarding process, about what success looks like in the first 90 days.

## Mistake 8: Underselling Projects on the Resume

Freshers often say "we built X" without explaining their specific contribution, the technical decisions made, or the outcome.

Fix: For every resume project, prepare answers for: What was your specific role? What was the hardest technical challenge? What would you do differently? What was the measurable impact?

## Mistake 9: Poor Time Management in the Aptitude Round

Spending 3–4 minutes on a single hard question while 10 easy questions go unattempted is one of the biggest placement test mistakes.

Fix: Set a strict 60–90 second limit per question. Flag and return. Bank easy marks first.

## Mistake 10: Treating Mock Interviews as Low Stakes

Candidates who treat mock interviews casually — pausing to look things up, restarting answers — do not build the skill they actually need under real pressure.

Fix: Every mock is a real interview. Simulate real conditions: sit up straight, no phone, commit to every answer even if imperfect.

## FAQ: Placement Interview Mistakes

### Q: What is the single most impactful change I can make for placement interviews?
A: Start practising out loud immediately. The gap between mental preparation and spoken performance is larger than most freshers realise.

### Q: How do I recover if I give a bad answer during a placement interview?
A: Acknowledge it briefly if the interviewer pushes back, then pivot to what you do know. Trying to defend a clearly wrong answer damages credibility more than the original mistake.

title: Amazon Placement Preparation 2026: SDE Roadmap & Interview Guide
author: PlacementDo Team
excerpt: A complete guide to cracking Amazon's Software Development Engineer (SDE) placement interviews. Covers the online assessment (OA), technical rounds, and Amazon's Leadership Principles.
content:
# Amazon Placement Preparation 2026: The Complete SDE Guide

Landing a Software Development Engineer (SDE-1) role at Amazon is the dream for many engineering freshers. Amazon's placement process is rigorous, focusing equally on hard technical skills (Data Structures and Algorithms) and cultural fit (Leadership Principles). Here is exactly how to prepare for Amazon campus placements in 2026.

## The Amazon Selection Process

Amazon's hiring process for freshers usually consists of 4 distinct stages:

1.  **Online Assessment (OA)**: Technical test on HackerRank/AMCAT platform.
2.  **Technical Interview 1**: Focus on medium-level DSA and core computer science.
3.  **Technical Interview 2**: Focus on hard DSA, code optimisation, and project deep dives.
4.  **Bar Raiser / Technical HR**: Behavioral questions integrated with technical problem solving.

## Stage 1: The Online Assessment (OA)

The Amazon OA is notoriously tough. You must clear this to even speak to an interviewer.

### What it includes:
- **Coding Section**: Usually 2 problems to be solved in 90 minutes. Difficulty ranges from LeetCode Medium to Hard.
- **Workstyles Assessment**: A behavioral test mapping your professional personality to Amazon's principles.
- **Debugging Section** (Sometimes): Fixing logical errors in 7-10 snippets of code within 20 minutes.

### How to prepare:
- **Master Graphs and DP**: The two coding questions almost always involve Graphs (BFS/DFS, Dijkstra), Dynamic Programming, or Sliding Window.
- **Be Honest on the Workstyles test**: Do not try to "game" it; answer consistently as someone who takes ownership and delivers results.

## Stage 2 & 3: The Technical Interviews

Amazon technical interviews are 45–60 minutes long. The interviewer will ask you to write production-ready code (not just pseudo-code) on a shared whiteboard or editor.

### Core Topics to Master:
1.  **Trees and BSTs**: Traversal, finding ancestors, balancing.
2.  **Hashing and Heaps**: Designing custom data structures (e.g., LRU Cache is an Amazon favorite).
3.  **Graphs**: Shortest path, topological sort, islands problems.
4.  **String Manipulation**: Anagrams, palindromes, substring problems.

### Amazon's "Code Quality" Expectation:
- Your code must compile (if using an IDE).
- Variables must be named clearly (no `i`, `j`, `x` except in short loops).
- You must handle edge cases (null inputs, empty arrays, large numbers) *before* the interviewer points them out.
- You must state the Time and Space Complexity (Big O) as soon as you finish writing the code.

## Stage 4: The Bar Raiser & Leadership Principles

This is where many technically brilliant candidates fail. Amazon uses 16 Leadership Principles (LPs) to evaluate every candidate. The interviewer known as the "Bar Raiser" ensures you are better than 50% of the currently employed engineers at that level.

### The Most Important LPs for Freshers:
- **Customer Obsession**: Start with the user and work backwards.
- **Ownership**: Taking responsibility for failures, not just successes.
- **Learn and Be Curious**: How quickly you adapt to new tech stacks.
- **Deliver Results**: Getting things done despite blockers.

### How to answer LP questions:
Use the **STAR method** (Situation, Task, Action, Result).

If asked: *"Tell me about a time you had to meet a tight deadline."*
- **Situation**: "During my final year project..."
- **Task**: "We had to deliver the MVP in 3 weeks instead of 6..."
- **Action**: "I rescoped the requirements, parallelised the database design with the frontend work, and put in weekend hours..."
- **Result**: "We delivered 2 days early and the client adopted our prototype."

## A 3-Month Amazon Target Plan

- **Month 1**: Solve top 100 "Amazon Tagged" questions on LeetCode. Focus on Trees, Graphs, and Hashmaps.
- **Month 2**: Write out STAR stories for at least 5 of Amazon's Leadership Principles. Practice writing code on a plain text editor without autocomplete.
- **Month 3**: Take strict 90-minute timed OA mock tests. Schedule at least 5 technical mock interviews.

*Pro Tip for Placement Prep:* Use PlacementDo's AI mock interview tool to simulate the Amazon Bar Raiser round and get specific feedback on your LP story structure.

## Conclusion

Cracking Amazon placement isn't about knowing obscure algorithms; it's about flawlessly executing standard DSA patterns and clearly communicating your problem-solving process. Start coding today, and do not ignore the Leadership Principles.
